mcqs.question: Why does speculative execution pay off on average, despite the risk of executing down the wrong path?
options: Because misprediction recovery has zero performance cost
Because modern branch predictors are right the large majority of the time, so most speculative work turns out to be exactly the useful work the program needed anyway
Because speculative instructions execute faster than non-speculative ones
Because speculation only happens when the CPU is otherwise idle
mcqs.explanation: Speculation is a bet, and it pays off because the bet is usually right — high predictor accuracy means most speculative work is genuinely useful work started early. Misprediction recovery does have a real cost (a flush), speculative instructions don't run at different speeds, and speculation happens continuously, not just when idle.

mcqs.question: What makes it safe for a CPU to speculatively execute instructions past an unresolved branch?
options: Speculative instructions run on a separate, isolated CPU core
Speculative results are held in temporary structures like the reorder buffer and never become visible architectural state until the branch is confirmed correct, so a misprediction just discards them
The compiler guarantees speculative code never has side effects
Speculative execution is disabled whenever a branch is present
mcqs.explanation: The safety net is that nothing speculative touches visible architectural state (registers, memory) until commit, so a wrong guess is simply discarded with no incorrect behavior ever observed. There's no separate core involved, compilers can't guarantee side-effect-free code in general, and speculation is precisely what happens across branches, not disabled by them.

mcqs.question: What is speculative load execution betting on?
options: That the load's target address will never change
That an earlier, not-yet-resolved store won't write to the same address the load is reading (won't alias), so it's safe to execute the load before the store's address is known
That the load will always execute faster than a store
That the CPU has no earlier stores at all
mcqs.explanation: Speculative load execution specifically bets against store-load aliasing, letting the load proceed before the store's address resolves; if the store does alias, the load and its dependents must be squashed and re-executed. It's not about the load's target changing, relative speed, or the absence of stores.

mcqs.question: What is the core insight behind Spectre-class attacks on speculative execution?
options: Speculative execution never actually rolls back architectural state, so wrong-path results are visible to programs directly

Even though architectural results are correctly rolled back, speculation can leave microarchitectural side effects (like cache state) that survive rollback and can be measured through timing to infer secret data
Speculative execution only affects floating-point instructions, which are exempt from security review
Branch prediction accuracy is the direct cause of all cache-timing vulnerabilities
mcqs.explanation: Spectre exploits the gap between architectural correctness (which is preserved) and microarchitectural state (which isn't rolled back) — a squashed speculative load can still leave data in cache, measurable via timing. Architectural rollback does happen correctly; the issue is unrelated to floating-point exemptions, and predictor accuracy isn't itself the vulnerability, the side channel is.
